art.text: In the western Central African Republic stand the Bouar Megaliths, which may have been developed between 3500 BCE and 2700 BCE, during the late Neolithic. They may be evidence of an advanced level of habitation.

Wavy-line pottery was produced between the 8th and 4th millennia BCE. Its spread stretched from the savanna to the eastern Saharan region, and from Mauritania to the Red Sea. This supports the conclusion that the regions traded with each other and were interconnected.

Dotted wavy-line pottery, produced between the 8th and 4th millennia BCE, spread across the Ennedi Plateau and Wadi Howar. It linked the regions of the Middle Nile River, Lake Chad, and the Benue-Niger River.
Wavy-line pottery turns up at several sites in Chad, including Delibo Cave, Jebel Eghei, and Tibesti. It also appears in Niger at Adrar Madet, though most of it was found in the Central Nile.

Potters in this tradition developed distinct styles. Wavy-line pottery developed six ceramic subvariants, while dotted wavy-line pottery developed three. Both were produced between the 8th and 4th millennia BCE.

science.text: The mutation for sickle cell originated in the Sahara or in the northwest forest region of western Central Africa, such as Cameroon. It arose at least 7,300 years ago, though possibly as early as 22,000 years ago, during the time of the Green Sahara. Sickle cell disease is counted among the genetic adaptations to malaria found throughout Sub-Saharan Africa, which may have initially developed 7300 years ago.

The Stone Age ended between 4000 BC and 2000 BC as metalworking arrived. In Sub-Saharan Africa it was followed directly by the Iron Age, and ironworking there was either invented independently or came across the Sahara from the north.

The Ishango bone, found in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is a bone tool with a quartz piece fixed to one end and three columns of ordered engravings. Some see it as a tally stick or counting tool. It was first estimated to date between 9,000 BCE and 6,500 BCE.

Around 10,000 years ago, Kalambo Falls was occupied by the Magosian culture, which in turn gave way to Wilton activity. The site, at the southeast end of Lake Tanganyika, is considered one of the most important archaeological sites in Africa.
Humans are thought to have lived at Ishango, on the Semliki River, from 20,000 to 5,000 BC. Dating the site's layers used Carbon-14 and the relative dating of stratigraphic layers.

Modern sickle cell haplotypes include the Cameroon/Central African Republic and Benin/Senegal types. The ancestral haplotype may have first arisen in the ancestors of modern West Africans, who carried haplogroups such as E1b1a1-M4732.

Dating the Ishango bone has been hard because nearby volcanic activity upset the ratio of carbon isotopes. Early estimates of 9,000 to 6,500 BCE were later replaced when the site was re-evaluated, and the bone is now thought to be about 20,000 years old.

In Africa the Neolithic was characterized mainly by herding societies rather than large agricultural ones. There was copper metallurgy and bronze smelting in Africa too, but archaeologists do not currently recognize a separate Copper Age or Bronze Age there.

culture.text: Around 10,000 years ago, hunter-gatherer groups ancestral to the San were already spread across a vast stretch of Africa, from Tanzania, Zambia and Angola down to Cape Agulhas at the continent's southern tip. This makes the San one of the oldest cultures on Earth.

At the Wilton rock shelter in South Africa, archaeologist Janette Deacon identified a stone tool industry dating to about 10,000 years ago, made up of large scrapers crafted from quartzite. These tools were found alongside the remains of large animals, suggesting the people who made them hunted big game.

The Pygmy hunter-gatherers of Central Africa are believed to descend from the region's earliest Middle Stone Age inhabitants. Starting about 5,500 years ago, they began to be partially absorbed or displaced by incoming agricultural peoples of the Central Sudanic and Ubangian phyla.

By about 8,000 years ago, the stone scrapers made by people at the Wilton rock shelter had grown much smaller, with only a few tool types still in use. Archaeologist Janette Deacon calls this shift the site's growth phase, or stage 1, of the Wilton stone tool tradition.

Bantu-speaking agriculturalists in the Grasslands of northwestern Cameroon began to migrate gradually south sometime between 5000 and 3000 BCE. Despite intensive research, the cause of the migrations and the directions taken are still unclear, though there were multiple dispersal events.
